body:
Background: The Ahmedabad Textile Industry

The Ahmedabad Mill Workers' Satyagraha of 1918 was an important early example of Gandhi applying satyagraha to an industrial labour dispute.

Ahmedabad in Gujarat was a major textile manufacturing centre. Its cotton mills employed large numbers of workers, many of whom depended on regular wages to support their families.

Unlike Champaran, where the principal opponents were European indigo planters, the Ahmedabad dispute involved Indian textile mill owners and their workers.

Causes of the Wage Dispute

During a plague epidemic in Ahmedabad in 1917, textile mills paid an additional allowance to encourage workers to remain employed. This payment became known as the plague bonus.

When the epidemic subsided, mill owners attempted to discontinue the bonus. However, the cost of essential commodities had risen, partly because of the economic conditions associated with the First World War. Workers therefore faced continuing financial difficulties despite the decline of the epidemic.

The workers wanted better wages, while the mill owners resisted the increase sought by the workers.

Different Wage Proposals

  • Workers' initial demand: A wage increase of 50%.
  • Mill owners' offer: A wage increase of 20%.
  • Gandhi's proposed settlement: A wage increase of 35%, which he considered reasonable after examining the dispute.

Gandhi's 35% figure was not simply the average of the workers' demand and the employers' offer. He supported it after considering the workers' circumstances and the justification for an increase.

Important Persons in the Movement

Anasuya Sarabhai

Anasuya Sarabhai was an important organiser of textile workers in Ahmedabad. She supported their demand for better wages and played a central role in mobilising workers during the dispute.

Ambalal Sarabhai

Ambalal Sarabhai, Anasuya Sarabhai's brother, was a prominent textile industrialist who represented the mill owners' side.

The relationship between Anasuya and Ambalal illustrates an important feature of the movement: the opposing parties were not divided by nationality. The dispute concerned the economic interests of industrial workers and employers within Indian society.

Mahatma Gandhi

Gandhi attempted to secure a fair settlement through discussion and arbitration. When negotiations failed, he supported disciplined collective action by the workers.

Organisation of the Nonviolent Strike

Gandhi advised the textile workers to maintain their demand peacefully and remain united. The workers undertook a pledge not to return to work until their demand was accepted or the dispute was referred to arbitration.

He emphasised several conditions for a successful strike:

  • Workers should not resort to violence against mill owners or other workers.
  • They should not intimidate workers who chose not to participate in the strike.
  • They should maintain their commitment without depending on charity for subsistence.
  • Where possible, they should undertake other honest work to support themselves during the strike.

Daily gatherings helped sustain the workers' morale. Their pledge became an important source of unity during the dispute.

Gandhi's Fast and the Settlement

As the strike continued, many workers experienced financial hardship. Some began losing confidence in their ability to maintain the protest.

Gandhi feared that the workers might abandon their pledge and that frustration could weaken the movement's nonviolent discipline.

On 15 March 1918, Gandhi began a fast to reinforce the workers' determination. The fast also placed moral pressure on the mill owners, with whom Gandhi maintained personal relationships.

After negotiations, the parties agreed to submit the dispute to arbitration. Gandhi ended his fast on 18 March 1918. The strike had lasted approximately 21 days.

Arbitration

Arbitration is a method of settling a dispute in which the parties submit their disagreement to an agreed third party for a decision. In Ahmedabad, it provided a way to resolve the wage dispute through an accepted decision rather than continued industrial confrontation.

Anandshankar Dhruva was appointed as arbitrator. The final award provided a 35% wage increase, corresponding to the demand supported by Gandhi.

The movement is therefore remembered for the combination of a peaceful strike, a personal fast and an arbitration settlement.

Longer-Term Importance in Gujarat

The Ahmedabad experience strengthened the development of organised labour activity in Gujarat. It showed that industrial workers could collectively negotiate their economic demands while maintaining nonviolent discipline.

The movement also contributed to the development of a more organised relationship between textile workers and their representatives.

In 1920, the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, popularly known as the Majoor Mahajan Sangh, was established. Anasuya Sarabhai was a central figure in its development. The organisation became an important institution associated with Ahmedabad's textile labour movement.

The wage dispute occurred in 1918, while the formal Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association was established in 1920. The 2 dates refer to related but distinct developments.

Significance for Gandhian Politics

The Ahmedabad movement demonstrated that satyagraha could be applied to an economic dispute between workers and employers, not only to a conflict involving the colonial government.

It also established negotiation and arbitration as important elements of Gandhi's approach to industrial disputes. His fast was intended to uphold the workers' pledge, although Gandhi himself recognised that it also exerted pressure on the mill owners.

Prelims focus

  • Year: 1918.
  • Place: Ahmedabad, Gujarat.
  • Participants: Cotton textile mill workers.
  • Main issue: Wage increase following the withdrawal of the plague bonus and continuing high living costs.
  • Important persons: Gandhi, Anasuya Sarabhai and Ambalal Sarabhai.
  • Wage figures: Workers initially sought 50%; employers offered 20%; the final award provided 35%.
  • Trap: Ahmedabad was an industrial labour movement, not a peasant land revenue movement.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part V, In Touch with Labour and The Fast, online text consulted 21 November 2026; NCERT, Class 8 History, Our Pasts III, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s-1947, printed p. 116, 2020-21 edition; Government of India, Ministry of Tourism, Press Information Bureau, Dekho Apna Desh Webinar Series on Gandhi, Ahmedabad and Salt March, 4 October 2020, consulted 21 November 2026; Six Decades of Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad (1917-1977), Appendix A, Chronicle of Main Events, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: Ahmedabad Mill Workers' Satyagraha, 1918: Wage Dispute, Nonviolent Strike and Arbitration

body:
Background: Agrarian Distress in Kheda

The Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 was a peasant movement in Gujarat led by Mahatma Gandhi with the important assistance of Vallabhbhai Patel and other local leaders.

The movement arose when cultivators in Kheda district suffered severe agricultural difficulties following crop failure. Many farmers were unable to meet the land revenue demanded by the colonial government.

Their immediate demand was relief from revenue collection during a period of agricultural distress.

Land Revenue and the Crop-Yield Rule

Under the colonial land revenue system, cultivators were required to pay an assessed amount to the government. A poor harvest could make payment difficult because agricultural income depended heavily on crop production.

The revenue rules contained provisions allowing collection to be suspended when the assessed harvest fell sufficiently below normal.

The Four-Anna Criterion

Gandhi described the relevant rule in terms of a crop assessment of 4 annas or less, measured against a normal crop valued at 16 annas.

This represented a crop assessment of 25% or less of normal.

The cultivators maintained that their crops fell below the required threshold and that they were therefore entitled to suspension of revenue collection.

The authorities disputed their assessment and continued demanding payment.

The 25% figure in Kheda referred to the crop-assessment threshold relevant to suspension of land revenue. It was not a 25% reduction in the land revenue rate.

Causes of the Movement

Several related difficulties created the conditions for the satyagraha:

  • Crop failure: Poor agricultural production reduced the ability of cultivators to pay government revenue.
  • Economic hardship: High prices and other difficulties increased the burden on rural households.
  • Revenue demands: Officials continued seeking payment despite cultivators' claims that the crop assessment justified relief.
  • Failure of representations: Petitions and requests for a reconsideration of the assessment did not secure the relief sought by the peasants.

The movement therefore focused on the relationship between agricultural distress and the government's insistence on collecting land revenue.

Role of Gandhi, Vallabhbhai Patel and the Gujarat Sabha

Gandhi's Leadership

Gandhi considered the farmers' case after inquiries and representations had already been made. He supported their demand that the government suspend the collection of revenue under the applicable rules.

When petitions and negotiations failed, he advised the cultivators to adopt satyagraha by collectively withholding the disputed revenue.

Vallabhbhai Patel

Vallabhbhai Patel, then a lawyer in Gujarat, became one of Gandhi's principal associates in the campaign.

Patel assisted in organising cultivators, maintaining their confidence and communicating the purpose of the movement. His participation in Kheda was an important stage in the development of his political leadership.

The Gujarat Sabha and Other Associates

The Gujarat Sabha was an important public organisation associated with the campaign. Gandhi was its president during the agitation. It submitted petitions and representations seeking relief for the cultivators.

Other participants and organisers included Mohanlal Pandya, Shankarlal Parikh and Indulal Yagnik. They contributed to the mobilisation and organisation of the peasants.

The movement maintained an important organisational centre at Nadiad in Kheda district.

The Decision to Withhold Land Revenue

The cultivators adopted a pledge to refrain voluntarily from paying the disputed land revenue until the government granted the requested suspension.

The pledge involved acceptance of legal consequences. Those participating understood that the authorities could seize property or take other steps to recover the revenue.

The movement also involved an important principle of collective responsibility. Even cultivators who could afford to pay were asked to support the protest because payment by wealthier farmers could weaken the position of poorer cultivators.

Poor peasants might otherwise be forced to borrow money or sell their belongings to satisfy the government's demands.

Collective Non-Payment

Kheda Satyagraha was based on the organised refusal to pay disputed land revenue. It was not a protest against compulsory indigo cultivation or a demand for higher industrial wages.

Government Response

The colonial authorities attempted to collect revenue despite the protest. Their measures included the attachment or seizure of crops, cattle and other property. In some cases, property was auctioned.

The cultivators were expected to maintain nonviolent discipline despite these measures.

The government and the satyagrahis consequently remained engaged in a dispute over whether revenue collection should continue under the prevailing agricultural conditions.

Settlement and Withdrawal of the Movement

The campaign began formally with the cultivators' pledge on 22 March 1918.

During the subsequent negotiations, the authorities indicated that collection would be suspended for poorer cultivators while those who were able to pay should pay their assessment.

A local order communicated on 3 June 1918 provided the basis for ending the agitation. Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel announced the conclusion of the struggle on 6 June 1918.

The settlement represented a limited achievement rather than an unconditional cancellation of land revenue for every cultivator. Gandhi later observed that the practical benefit of the suspension had not reached many of the poorer farmers.

Suspension and remission are not identical. Suspension postpones collection, while remission cancels the amount due. The Kheda settlement primarily concerned suspension of collection for poorer cultivators, not a general permanent cancellation of every farmer's revenue liability.

Importance of the Kheda Movement

Kheda demonstrated the ability of Gujarat's peasants to organise around a specific economic grievance and challenge the implementation of colonial revenue demands.

It strengthened the relationship between Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel and expanded the role of local public workers in rural political activity.

The movement also showed that organised non-payment could be used as a form of nonviolent resistance when a demand for administrative relief had failed through ordinary representations.

For Gandhi, the practical achievements of the movement were limited, but the experience contributed to the political education and growing self-confidence of Gujarat's cultivators.

Prelims focus

  • Year: 1918.
  • Place: Kheda district, Gujarat.
  • Main grievance: Collection of land revenue despite crop failure and claims for relief.
  • Revenue criterion: A crop assessment of 4 annas or less out of 16 annas represented 25% or less of normal.
  • Important persons: Gandhi, Vallabhbhai Patel, Mohanlal Pandya and Indulal Yagnik.
  • Important organisation: Gujarat Sabha.
  • Trap: Kheda's outcome was conditional revenue suspension for poorer cultivators, not a universal cancellation of land revenue.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part V, The Kheda Satyagraha and End of Kheda, online texts consulted 21 November 2026; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Kheda - June 1918, chronology entries for 3 June and 6 June, consulted 21 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12 History, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Theme 13, printed p. 349, 2018-19 edition; Government of Tamil Nadu, State Council of Educational Research and Training, Class 12 History, Volume 1, Unit 4, Advent of Gandhi and Mass Mobilisation, printed pp. 43-45, 2019 edition.]
